planting.note: Press offsets onto the surface of lean, gritty, extremely well-drained soil in full sun in spring or fall.

directions: Royal Ruby is a compact, heavily colored hens-and-chicks cultivar whose rosettes flush deep wine-red to near-burgundy across most of the leaf, intensifying with cold nights and strong sun exposure rather than fading like many green-based cultivars. Set offsets directly onto lean, sharply drained gravelly soil, since any organic richness or standing moisture quickly causes rot at the root crown. It multiplies steadily by short-stemmed offsets, filling crevices and trough plantings within a couple of seasons without becoming invasive. Each individual rosette blooms once on a short stalk and dies afterward, but the surrounding chicks continue the clump indefinitely.

planting.note: Press offsets onto the surface of lean, gravelly, very well-drained soil in full sun in spring or fall.

directions: Cleveland Morgan is an older, well-established sempervivum hybrid noted for its bicolor rosette, with green leaf bases shading sharply into deep brick-red to maroon tips, giving mature clumps a striking dual-tone appearance most vivid in cool weather. Plant offsets on the surface of sharply drained, mineral-rich soil, since it needs almost no organic matter and rots quickly if kept damp. It offsets freely and fills rock garden pockets, wall crevices, and trough plantings within a season or two. Full sun keeps the color contrast sharp; in shade the rosettes stretch and lose their red tipping.

common_name: Ruby Heart Chick Charms Hens and Chicks

planting.note: Press small offsets onto the surface of lean, extremely well-drained gritty soil in full sun in spring.

directions: Ruby Heart is part of the compact Chick Charms breeding line developed for small-container and fairy-garden use, forming tight, saucer-sized rosettes with rose-pink to ruby coloring that deepens through the growing season. Because rosettes stay small compared to older heirloom sempervivum cultivars, close spacing in shallow troughs, strawberry jars, or miniature rock gardens works well. Plant offsets directly on the surface of sharply drained gritty mix, since even brief waterlogging causes rot in the compact crown. It multiplies quickly by offsets and holds its color best with full sun and lean soil.

planting.note: Plant stem cuttings or nursery stock in fast-draining, gritty soil in bright light to part shade; strongest variegation develops in bright but not scorching sun.

directions: Sunburst is a widely grown variegated form of tree aeonium, its flat rosettes striped in cream, soft yellow, and green with a pink blush along the leaf margins that intensifies in cooler weather and brighter light. Like other aeoniums it follows a winter-growing, summer-dormant cycle, so water moderately through fall, winter, and spring and taper off in summer heat when growth slows. Grow in fast-draining, lean soil in bright light to light afternoon shade in hot climates, since harsh, unfiltered midday sun can scorch the pale variegated tissue. Propagate easily from stem cuttings allowed to callus for a few days before setting into dry mix, and remove any all-green reverted shoots promptly to keep the variegation stable.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Plant container stock in well-drained, lean soil in bright light to part shade during the cool growing season.

directions: Canary Island velvet rose forms one of the largest single rosettes in the aeonium genus, often reaching well over a foot across, covered in short, soft, velvety hairs that give the pale green to yellow-green leaves a distinctive suede-like texture and sheen. It is nearly stemless, hugging the ground as a solitary rosette or small cluster rather than branching into a shrub like tree aeonium. Grow in lean, fast-draining soil with bright light to light shade, watering through the cool winter and spring growing season and reducing water sharply during summer dormancy. Its large size and soft texture make it a strong focal specimen in a succulent bed or oversized container, best appreciated where it can be viewed up close.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Plant stem cuttings or nursery stock in fast-draining, gritty soil in full sun to part shade; darkest color develops with strong, cool-season light.

directions: Cyclops is a hybrid aeonium prized for its huge single rosette, often close to a foot across, combining a deep burgundy-black outer zone with a bright lime-green center that creates a bold two-toned target pattern unlike almost any other succulent. Grow in fast-draining, lean soil in full sun to light afternoon shade in hot inland climates, following the same winter-growing, summer-semi-dormant rhythm as other aeoniums. Water regularly through the cool season and taper off in summer heat, and expect some leaf drop and stress during the hottest months even with good care. Propagate from stem or offset cuttings allowed to callus before rooting; established plants make dramatic single-specimen focal points in containers or succulent beds.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Plant offsets or rooted stem sections in gritty, well-drained mix in bright, indirect light to part shade, ideally against a support the stems can scramble over.

directions: Unlike almost every other gasteria, which grows as a low, stemless rosette, climbing gasteria produces long, trailing to scrambling stems set with small, tongue-shaped, warty leaves that lean and clamber over rocks or neighboring shrubs in its native South African habitat. Grow it in bright, indirect light or part shade in gritty, fast-draining mix, and provide a low trellis, rock face, or hanging container so the lax stems have something to drape over or climb through. Water only when the soil has dried, since like other gasterias it is highly rot-prone in constantly damp conditions, and it tolerates lower light better than most succulents. Propagate readily from stem cuttings or by rooting fallen stem sections, and expect slow, steady growth into an unusual sprawling specimen rather than a tidy rosette.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Plant offsets in very well-drained, gritty mix in bright, indirect light to part shade; this species offsets rapidly and forms dense mats rather than a single rosette.

directions: Clustered gasteria is among the most vigorously offsetting species in the genus, quickly forming dense, low mats of small, thick, tongue-shaped rosettes rather than staying as a single specimen, making it well suited to shallow bowls or as a groundcover among taller succulents. Grow in bright, indirect light or part shade in fast-draining, gritty mix, since it naturally grows tucked into rocky crevices and scrub shade in South Africa and scorches in intense, unfiltered sun. Water only when the soil is fully dry, and separate and repot congested clumps every couple of years to keep individual rosettes from crowding each other out. Slender arching stalks of small pink-orange tubular flowers appear over an extended season on established clumps.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; avoid wetting the fuzzy leaves.

directions: Bear's Claw is a distinct, smaller-leaved cousin of the better-known Bear's Paw, covered in dense, soft gray-green fuzz and tipped along the leaf margin with several small reddish-brown teeth that curl slightly inward, resembling a claw rather than a flat paw pad. Grow in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix, and water only once the soil has dried completely, since the fuzzy leaves are especially prone to rot and unsightly spotting if kept wet or splashed during watering. It branches and sprawls somewhat more than Bear's Paw, eventually forming a small shrubby clump that roots easily from stem or leaf cuttings allowed to callus for a few days first. An easy, conversation-piece succulent for a bright windowsill or dry container planting.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference
